The Indian skipper frog Euphlyctis cyanophlyctis commences its life cycle within a gelatinous egg mass, where each fertilised ovum develops into an embryo nourished by its yolk reserves. Upon eclosion, the newly emerged larva is remarkably small, possessing a wet weight at birth of only 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams]. This initial mass reflects the modest egg diameter of roughly 1.5 millimetres characteristic of the species. The endotrophic tadpole then undergoes rapid growth through the aquatic larval phase, transitioning to exogenous feeding as it develops into an actively grazing tadpole. Metamorphosis, a critical morphological transformation encompassing tail resorption and limb bud development, occurs when the individual attains a snout-vent length of approximately 2.5 centimetres . At this point, female froglets typically weigh around 1.4 grams , whereas their male counterparts are slightly lighter at about 1.2 grams . This disparity in mass at the larval-juvenile transition establishes an early foundation for the sexual size dimorphism that becomes increasingly pronounced as the animals progress toward adulthood. The entire developmental sequence from egg to metamorphosis is completed over a period of several months, depending on local thermal conditions and resource availability in the temporary monsoon pools.

Juvenile Euphlyctis cyanophlyctis embark on a sustained period of somatic growth, gradually approaching their definitive adult dimensions. The ultimate snout-vent length for females reaches 7 centimetres [Li = 7 centimetres], while males attain a smaller maximum of 5.5 centimetres [Li = 5.5 centimetres]. This divergence in maximal linear size is paralleled by a substantial difference in ultimate wet weight, with females reaching an asymptotic body mass of 31 grams [Wwi = 31 grams] and males peaking at 12.5 grams [Wwi = 12.5 grams]. Such marked sexual size dimorphism is well-documented in dicroglossid frogs and is often interpreted as a consequence of fecundity selection favouring larger females capable of producing more eggs per clutch. Field surveys across the Indian subcontinent have confirmed these upper bounds, with the largest recorded specimens aligning closely with these values. The growth trajectory from a recently metamorphosed froglet to a full-sized adult spans several years and is strongly modulated by both prey availability and ambient thermal conditions, particularly in the temporary water bodies these frogs frequently inhabit during the monsoon season.

The onset of gonadal maturation defines a pivotal transition in the life history of this species. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 26 °C [T = 26 °C], female Euphlyctis cyanophlyctis reach sexual maturity 242 days following metamorphosis [tp = 242 days following metamorphosis]. At this pubertal stage, females measure approximately 5.2 centimetres [Lp = approximately 5.2 centimetres] in snout-vent length and carry a wet weight of roughly 12.8 grams [Wwp = roughly 12.8 grams]. Males undergo this developmental milestone considerably faster, attaining puberty just 91 days after completing metamorphosis [tp = 91 days after completing metamorphosis] at the same ambient temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. The corresponding snout-vent length at puberty for males is 4 centimetres [Lp = 4 centimetres], and their wet weight at this juncture averages around 6.1 grams [Wwp = around 6.1 grams]. The pronounced sex-specific difference in the timing of reproductive maturation likely reflects the divergent selective pressures operating on males, where early access to breeding aggregations confers a competitive advantage in amplexus acquisition.

Reproductive output in the Indian skipper frog reaches notable levels during the peak monsoon months. A typically sized female with a snout-vent length of 5.7 centimetres deposits approximately 551 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 551 eggs per clutch], as documented by Gram in 2009 under a thermal regime of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. Importantly, individual females are capable of producing multiple clutches within a single breeding season, with field observations indicating that they may generate around nine distinct clutches annually [F_R_i = around nine distinct clutches annually]. The combination of a substantial clutch size with a relatively high annual clutch frequency yields a considerable per capita reproductive rate, enabling populations to rebound quickly following the dry season. The eggs themselves are deposited in shallow, rain-fed pools where the water temperature typically hovers near 26 °C [T = 26 °C], promoting consistent developmental rates. This reproductive strategy, characterised by high fecundity partitioned across several discrete events, is typical of many aquatic-breeding anurans inhabiting seasonally unpredictable environments.

The natural lifespan of Euphlyctis cyanophlyctis under field conditions has been estimated through mark-recapture studies and long-term monitoring of captive cohorts. At a stable temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C], the maximum longevity recorded for this species is roughly 5 years [am = roughly 5 years], a value consistent with those reported for other small-bodied dicroglossid frogs occupying similar semi-aquatic habitats. This comparatively modest lifespan is typical of anurans that exhibit rapid early growth and early reproductive maturation, channeling resources into reproduction rather than extended somatic persistence. Survival probabilities are highest during the post-metamorphic juvenile stage and decline steadily as individuals accumulate the physiological costs of repeated breeding efforts. Ultimately, natural mortality arises from senescence and progressive physiological deterioration, with few individuals surviving beyond their fifth year even under optimal captive conditions. The integration of these life-history parameters—from the minute 0.0018 gram [Wwb = 0.0018 gram] hatchling to the 31 gram [Wwi = 31 gram] adult female—illustrates a coherent energetic strategy finely tuned to the seasonal rhythms of the Indian subcontinent's aquatic ecosystems.
